The three OAuth glyphs used across the other eight files are the same three every time and are the obvious first candidates to inline, which alone removes react-icons from eight of the nine importers.

title: eslint-config-next is on major 16 while next is on major 15, so the lint rule set targets a framework major the app is not running
description: package.json:95 pins `next: 15.5.23`; package.json:131 pins `eslint-config-next: 16.3.2`, which in turn hard-depends on `@next/eslint-plugin-next: 16.3.2` (per the lockfile entry for eslint-config-next). The jump was deliberate and is explained at eslint.config.mjs:3-6: eslint-config-next 16 is the first release with native flat config, so moving to it let the repo drop the `@eslint/eslintrc` FlatCompat shim, and eslint.config.mjs:13 imports `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` directly. The side effect is that the Next-specific rules being enforced are the Next 16 set: rules added or changed for Next 16 conventions run against a Next 15 codebase, and rules removed in 16 for patterns Next 15 still has are not enforced at all. This also puts the two out of dependabot's `next-stack` group's reach as a unit, since .github/dependabot.yml:75-77 ignores `next` majors while `eslint-config-next` has already taken one.
impact: Bounded and mostly latent: the lint job either flags a Next 16 idiom the app cannot adopt yet, or stops flagging a Next 15 anti-pattern because the rule was dropped in 16. Neither breaks the build, but it means the `lint` gate's Next coverage is not the coverage the running framework needs, and there is no signal anywhere that says so.
recommendation: Add a comment at package.json:131 (or in eslint.config.mjs beside the import at line 13) recording that eslint-config-next is intentionally one major ahead of next and why, so the next person to read the manifest does not treat it as a mistake or 'fix' it downward. Revisit when the Next 16 upgrade lands and the two realign.

title: db:restore feeds GCM plaintext into psql before the auth tag is verified, so a corrupted or tampered backup is partially applied before the integrity check fails
description: For an .enc backup, runRestore builds `pipeline(source, decipher, decrypted)` at line 84 and immediately assigns the PassThrough to `source` (line 88), then at line 106 pipes it through gunzip into psql's stdin. AES-256-GCM emits plaintext as it decrypts and only validates the auth tag set at line 82 when the final block is processed, so by the time an authentication failure surfaces, every preceding block has already been gunzipped and executed by psql. The failure handler (line 85) prints "Decryption failed" and calls process.exit(1), leaving the already-executed statements committed, since psql is running without --single-transaction (see migrate-04).
impact: The whole point of authenticating the backup is to guarantee that a modified or truncated dump is never applied. As written, an attacker who can modify a backup file, or plain bit rot in cold storage, results in a partially applied dump plus an error message, rather than a clean refusal. Low severity because it requires an already-compromised or corrupted backup artifact, and because the operator does see a failure message.
recommendation: Decrypt and verify to a temporary file first, and only start psql once the decipher stream has ended without error, deleting the temp file in a finally. Alternatively keep the streaming path but combine it with `--single-transaction` on psql (already recommended in migrate-04) so a late decryption failure rolls back everything that was streamed.

title: The four manifests disagree about Node: cli declares >=18 (EOL since April 2025) while root and extension declare >=22, marketing declares nothing, and CI only ever runs the CLI on Node 22
description: `cli/package.json:16` declares `"node": ">=18"`, `package.json:8` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, `extension/package.json:9` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, and `marketing/package.json` declares no `engines` field at all. The Node 18 claim is repeated to users in three places: `cli/README.md:5` ("no dependencies (Node 18+ for global fetch)"), `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4` ("No dependencies: Node 18+ (global fetch) is all it needs"), and the docs page at `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95` ("It needs Node 18 or newer"). Node 18 reached end of life on 2025-04-30 and receives no security updates. It is also never exercised: the only place the CLI runs in CI is `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110`, `node --test` with `working-directory: cli`, inside the `test` job whose `setup-node` step pins `node-version: "22"` (line 47). So the supported-floor claim is asserted in three user-facing places and validated in none. Node's own `--test` runner also behaved differently in 18 (experimental, narrower default file-glob) than in 22, so `node --test` with no path argument is not guaranteed to discover `cli/vulnradar.test.mjs` there.
impact: A user or a CI pipeline pinned to Node 18 follows the documented floor, runs the CLI on a runtime that has had no security patches for over a year, and hits any regression alone because nothing tests that version. Meanwhile a contributor who reads the root manifest reasonably assumes Node 22 is the repo-wide floor and may use a Node 20-or-22-only API in cli/lib.mjs without any check catching it.
recommendation: Raise `cli/package.json:16` to `">=20"` (the oldest Node still in maintenance) or to `">=22"` to match the other three manifests, and update the three copy sites: `cli/README.md:5`, the header comment at `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4`, and `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95`. If Node 18 support is genuinely wanted, add a matrix entry to the CLI test step in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110` that runs `node --test` on 18 as well. Also add `"engines": { "node": ">=22.0.0" }` to `marketing/package.json` so all four agree.

title: jspdf and jspdf-autotable are production dependencies with zero imports, and vitest plus @vitest/coverage-v8 are in dependencies rather than devDependencies
description: package.json:92-93 declares jspdf 4.2.1 and jspdf-autotable 5.0.8 as runtime dependencies. A repo-wide grep for jspdf/jsPDF across every .ts, .tsx and .mjs outside node_modules, .next and the stale worktree returns exactly one hit, and it is a comment: tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 ('browser-rendering dependency here despite jspdf being in package.json for'). Nothing imports either package. Separately, @vitest/coverage-v8 4.1.11 (package.json:81) and vitest 4.1.11 (package.json:117) are listed under `dependencies` rather than devDependencies, so `npm ci --omit=dev` in a Docker build installs the whole test runner and its v8 coverage toolchain into the production image.
impact: Three unnecessary packages are installed, audited and shipped in every production install and Docker image. The two jspdf packages are also a live supply-chain surface for code that does not exist, and their presence implies a PDF export path that a reader of package.json would go looking for.
recommendation: Remove jspdf and jspdf-autotable from package.json dependencies (and update the comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8), and move vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 from dependencies to devDependencies. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents.

title: GitHub AI repo-review endpoint makes real GitHub API calls before its quota/rate gate
description: POST /api/v3/scan/github calls getRepoInfo and listRepoTree (real GitHub API requests using the user's connected token) before checkGithubReviewQuota runs. Every other AI-adjacent or expensive endpoint in this app (chat, verify, verify-batch, bulk scan, crawl, discover, demo-scan, browser sessions) goes through checkRateLimit first; this one has no per-request throttle at all, only a per-day quota check that happens after the two GitHub API round-trips. Impact is mostly limited to the calling user's own GitHub API rate limit rather than a shared resource, so this is low severity, but it's the one gap in an otherwise consistently-applied pattern. Evidence: app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts lines 73-119 (getRepoInfo/listRepoTree calls precede the checkGithubReviewQuota call at line 116); no import of checkRateLimit anywhere in that file (confirmed via grep, contrasted with every sibling route under app/api/v3/scan/).
recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Add a checkRateLimit gate (a new named limit, e.g. githubReview) at the top of the handler, before any GitHub API call, mirroring the pattern already used everywhere else.

title: Badge stats endpoint compares the share token in plaintext against scan_history.share_token instead of the hashed lookup used identically elsewhere, and silently ignores host_badges auto-updating tokens
description: app/api/v3/badge/[token]/stats/route.ts queries `WHERE sh.share_token = $1` (the raw plaintext token from the URL) rather than hashing it and comparing against share_token_hash, unlike the sibling badge image route (app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts) and the shared-report route (app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts), both of which deliberately hash first with a comment citing AUDIT-004#secrets-01 ('so the plaintext token is never compared directly in the DB'). Since share_token_hash is a Postgres GENERATED column computed from share_token in the same row, this isn't a new confidentiality gap (the plaintext already lives in that row either way) and 256 bits of entropy makes any timing-based guessing attack infeasible regardless -- so this is a consistency/defense-in-depth gap, not a demonstrated exploit path. Separately, this endpoint never queries host_badges at all, so it silently 404s for any of the new auto-updating badge tokens created via POST /api/v3/badge/site -- a functional gap parallel to the two routes it's supposed to mirror. Evidence: app/api/v3/badge/[token]/stats/route.ts:19-25 (`WHERE sh.share_token = $1`, no hashing, no host_badges fallback) vs. app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:39-73 and app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts:24-60 (both hash-then-compare and both fall back to host_badges).
recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Hash the incoming token with SHA-256 and compare against share_token_hash for consistency with the two sibling routes, and add the same host_badges fallback query so stats work for auto-updating badges too.

title: Container, IaC, cloud and SCA scanning and an IAST agent are real competitor features that this product should deliberately never build, and saying so is part of the answer
category: list (a) ranks 16 to 18: the deliberate do-not-build list
description: Three capabilities appear in the peer set and belong at the bottom of the ranking with a stated reason rather than in a backlog. (1) Container, IaC, cloud and SCA scanning: Snyk is the only vendor of the eight spanning SAST, SCA, container, IaC, secrets, DAST and SBOM, and the best tool in that space is Trivy, which is free, Apache-2.0, 37,679 stars, emits SARIF 2.1.0 and CycloneDX/SPDX, and would take years to match. VulnRadar's nearest existing capability is deliberately narrow and correct: lib/scanner/github-repo-scan.ts:1 reuses the secrets-extended detectors verbatim against repo file contents, and lib/scanner/software-inventory.ts plus osv-check.ts correlate detected libraries against OSV for the live URL. (2) An IAST agent: only Acunetix ships one (AcuSensor, for PHP, ASP.NET, Java and Node.js), and none of the other seven has a comparable server-side sensor. It would require a per-runtime agent, an installation story, and version support forever, and it directly contradicts the product's own repeated promise that there is nothing to deploy alongside your application (components/landing/landing-features.tsx:4, app/checks/page.tsx's "0 agents to install"). (3) An internal or behind-the-firewall scanning agent, which Snyk and Intruder both ship as a Docker or Kubernetes workload: for this product the self-host path is the answer to that requirement and is strictly better, since the whole scanner runs inside the network rather than a relay.
impact: None if left alone. The risk this finding addresses is the opposite one: each of these is impressive on a competitor's feature matrix, and a small team that chases them spends quarters reaching parity in a market it is not in, while the cheap items in comp-02, comp-03, comp-04, comp-06 and comp-07 stay unbuilt.
recommendation: Record all three as permanent non-goals in AGENTS.md or a short ROADMAP note so they stop reappearing. For (1), do the interop instead of the feature: document the pairing in app/docs ("Trivy for images and dependencies, VulnRadar for the deployed URL"), and since both emit SARIF 2.1.0, both already land in the same GitHub Security tab with no work. For (3), make the self-host answer explicit on the relevant /alternatives rows rather than building an agent: "They give you a relay container. This runs the whole scanner inside your network." That claim depends on comp-01 being fixed first.

title: AI answer engines cannot reach any of this because Cloudflare AI Crawl Control blocks them at the edge, which is a dashboard toggle and not a code change
description: Recorded so nobody spends a day on it in code. The app does its part: app/robots.ts and app/llms.txt/route.ts exist, lib/config/public-paths.ts explicitly allowlists /llms.txt, /llms-full.txt, /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml for session-less crawlers with a comment explaining that AI crawlers carry no cookie, and components/seo/structured-data.tsx emits SoftwareApplication and FAQPage JSON-LD on the landing page including both extension store URLs. None of that reaches an AI crawler, because Cloudflare's Managed robots.txt / AI Crawl Control feature overrides the application's own robots.txt at the edge and disallows GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot and Google-Extended. This was confirmed in prior work as the reason AI assistants do not know the product exists. It is fixed by turning the feature off in the Cloudflare dashboard. Related and separately filed: AUDIT-012#fe-01 found the root layout's await headers() forces all 311 routes dynamic so Cloudflare caches no HTML, which affects crawl budget for the roughly 780 SEO pages, and AUDIT-013#subdeps-01 found the npm name vulnradar is unclaimed while /docs/cli advertises npx vulnradar.
impact: None directly. It explains why the marketing surface described in the other findings does not appear in AI answers, and it prevents a future auditor from proposing code fixes for an edge configuration problem.
recommendation: No code change. The owner toggles Managed robots.txt / AI Crawl Control off in the Cloudflare dashboard for vulnradar.dev. Once that is done, the llms.txt and JSON-LD work already in the repo starts being read, and mkt-07's APP_DESCRIPTION rewrite becomes the sentence AI answers actually quote, which is a reason to do mkt-07 before or alongside the toggle.

title: Route-level loading and error boundaries are missing on 61 of 71 pages, but almost every gap is already covered by an in-page state ladder, so the real exposure is narrower than the raw count suggests

The 17 pages that are async server components (all of /legal, /tools, /alternatives, /checks, /security, /landing) resolve from the local registry and config rather than the database, so a missing loading.tsx there costs a paint, not a hang. The genuinely uncovered blocking surfaces are the ones filed separately above and in AUDIT-011#auth-08 (/login, /signup, /reset-password prerender `Suspense fallback={null}`) and #ck-06 (/contact's ticket list returns null while loading). Recorded so the next audit does not re-derive the 61-page number as if it were 61 blank screens.
impact: None directly. This is a negative result: the loading.tsx count understates the product's actual coverage, and prioritising by that count alone would spend effort on static pages while the real blank-screen and never-resolving cases (state-04, state-06, state-08) sit elsewhere.
recommendation: When acting on AUDIT-011#drift-13, prioritise error.tsx over loading.tsx: the segments that most need a boundary are /host/[hostname], /shared/[token] and /browser/[id], where a render-time throw on untrusted server data currently escapes to the full-screen app/error.tsx and destroys the public page chrome. loading.tsx can be skipped entirely for the 17 async server pages.

title: There are no actionable TODO/FIXME/HACK/XXX markers and no commented-out code blocks anywhere in the source: all 14 marker matches are scanner detection patterns or display placeholders

description: Item 6 of the scope expected 14 TODO-family markers across app, lib, components, extension/src, cli and scripts. All 14 matches exist, and none is a deferred-work marker. impact: None: this is a clean result. It is recorded so a later audit does not spend the same effort re-deriving it, and so the 14 raw grep hits are not mistaken for a backlog. If the owner wants to keep it that way, add 'no-warning-comments' at warn level for terms TODO/FIXME/HACK to eslint.config.mjs, scoped to app/, lib/, components/ and hooks/, and exclude lib/scanner/checks/ where those strings are detection data rather than notes.

title: npm audit is clean, every package resolves from the public registry, and the lockfile's Linux native bindings are intact
description: Recording the negative results so the next audit does not redo them. `npm audit --json` on the full tree reports 0 vulnerabilities across 813 packages (369 prod, 363 dev, 137 optional, 1 peer) at every severity including info, so there is no reachability analysis to do: nothing is reported. `npm view <pkg> deprecated` across all 86 direct dependencies returns nothing, and no lockfile entry carries a `deprecated` field. recommendation: No change. When applying any of the package.json edits in this section, re-run the Linux-binding check afterwards: the thirteen entries listed above must still be present in package-lock.json before the change is committed.

title: Sixteen packages are behind, and only next and typescript are majors: both are deliberately held, and the rest are minor or patch drift with no security content
description: `npm outdated --json` lists sixteen entries. Two are majors and both are held on purpose, documented in .github/dependabot.yml:73-81. Next 15.5.23 is well past the 15.2.3 that fixed the middleware-bypass advisory and npm audit reports nothing against it, so this is a planning item, not a security one, though see deps-13 for the eslint-config-next half of it having already moved. (b) `typescript` 6.0.3 vs 7.0.2 (package.json:135), held because `@typescript-eslint/*` 8.67.0 declares `typescript: ">=4.8.4 <6.1.0"`, so TS 7 would break both the lint and typecheck CI jobs; dependabot.yml:78-81 states exactly this. recommendation: No action needed on the fourteen minors beyond letting dependabot's weekly PRs land. Add a dated note to the typescript ignore rule at .github/dependabot.yml:78-81 so the hold is revisited rather than becoming permanent, and treat the Next 16 upgrade as its own scheduled piece of work given deps-13 shows the lint half already moved ahead of it.

title: SQL, XSS, path-traversal, command-injection, deserialization and secret-exposure surfaces were swept clean this pass, so the next audit can skip re-deriving them
category: injection surfaces verified clean (scope note, no action required)
description:
Recorded so this ground is not re-walked. SQL: every pool.query interpolation site was opened. The only dynamic SQL fragments are whitelist-derived (app/api/v3/admin/features/route.ts:210-230 filters against an ALLOWED_COLUMNS Set; lib/auth/authorization.ts:292 derives both table and owner column from the OWNERSHIP map; app/api/v3/history/[id]/route.ts:339-357 and app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:301-315 build SET clauses from server-side literals only; app/api/v3/ai/conversations/route.ts:155-178 and app/api/v3/admin/support-tickets/route.ts:35-45 build WHERE from validated enums). No dynamic ORDER BY, no `IN (${...})` list building, no string-concatenated table names. lib/domains/scope.ts:50 uses a DB value as a LIKE right-hand side, but lib/domains/verification.ts:45 constrains it to `^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$`.

XSS: only three dangerouslySetInnerHTML sites exist outside the scanner's own detection strings (components/ui/chart.tsx:82 config-derived, app/layout.tsx:158 a nonce'd bootstrap over JSON.stringify'd constants, components/seo/structured-data.tsx:57 through safeJsonLd's `<`/`>`/`&` escape). No innerHTML anywhere in extension/src. Every notification/scan-result href sink goes through safeHref (lib/ui/utils.ts:19). Emails escape scan data (lib/email/email.ts:1305, :1375, :1462, :1538). Markdown/compliance exports escape via lib/reports/md-escape.ts; the PDF writer escapes `\`, `(`, `)` at lib/reports/pdf-report.ts:51; SARIF is JSON.stringify.

Path traversal: avatars are BYTEA rows, not files (lib/uploads/avatar-storage.ts), and the upload path enforces a PNG/JPEG MIME plus magic-bytes allowlist (app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:255-290). app/api/v3/ai/context/route.ts:18-25 joins only fixed literal segments. app/api/v3/admin/backup/route.ts has no download-by-name. The updater extracts with `tar -xzf -C <tmp>` after checksum and cosign verification (lib/updater/apply.ts:178-189).

Command injection: the only child_process users are lib/updater/exec.ts, lib/backup/run-backup.ts and scripts/, all argv arrays with `shell: false`. No eval, new Function, vm, or request-derived dynamic import anywhere in app/, lib/, components/ or extension/src.

Prototype pollution: no recursive merge helper exists; the one `{...updates}` spread of a request body (app/api/v3/admin/features/route.ts:203) is filtered through an allowlist Set immediately after.

Secrets: no hardcoded credentials outside scanner test fixtures and docs placeholders; the only NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars hold an app URL, a Turnstile site key, a Stripe publishable key and SEO verification tokens; no token/secret/password value is passed to console.*; no route returns a secret column (lib/history/resolve-scan.ts:61 does `SELECT *` but every caller projects explicit fields).
impact: None. This is a coverage record.
recommendation: No action. If a future change adds a dynamic ORDER BY, a raw-HTML markdown renderer, a filesystem-backed upload path, or a recursive config merge, re-open the corresponding item above.
